passages.passage_text:
For several decades, a small set of laboratory findings has been cited as evidence that free will is an illusion. In the best known of these experiments, volunteers were asked to flex a wrist whenever they felt the urge and to note the position of a rapidly moving clock hand at the moment they became aware of deciding. Electrodes on the scalp registered a slow negative drift in electrical activity, the readiness potential, that began roughly half a second before movement and well before the reported moment of decision. Many commentators inferred that if the brain begins preparing an act before the agent is aware of choosing it, the choice was made by neural machinery, and consciousness merely watches.

The argument rests heavily on a narrow empirical base, so its parts should be separated. The first is the claim that the readiness potential marks a decision. This has been challenged by researchers who point out that when the signal is averaged across many trials, it is aligned to the movement, a procedure that can manufacture a gradual ramp out of random fluctuations. On this account, spontaneous neural noise crosses a threshold at an unpredictable moment, and the act follows; the ramp reflects nothing more than what such fluctuations look like when they are selected backward from their outcome. If so, the early signal is not a hidden verdict awaiting delivery but a background condition that makes a movement more likely without settling it.

The second part is the claim that the reported time of awareness is trustworthy. Judging a clock hand's position is retrospective estimation, which shifts with attention and expectation. A finding that awareness of deciding lags brain activity by a few hundred milliseconds may therefore say as much about the unreliability of introspective timing as about the causal order of events.

The third and most important part is the move from the laboratory to ordinary life. The tasks in question were deliberately arbitrary: nothing hung on whether the wrist moved now or a moment later. Yet the choices that matter to those who defend free will, such as whether to change careers, involve extended deliberation, the weighing of reasons, and revision in light of argument. To generalize from one to the other is to assume that all decisions are of the same kind, which is exactly what needs to be shown.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that neuroscience is irrelevant to the debate. Defenders of free will have often spoken as though the self were a command post standing outside the causal order of the brain and issuing orders to it. Evidence that conscious experience arrives late, or that unconscious processes shape which options even come to mind, damages this picture. But it damages only a particular version of the picture. Compatibilists have long held that freedom consists not in escaping causation but in acting from one's own reasons, remaining responsive to considerations that bear on what to do, and being able to revise one's course when those considerations change. On this view, to discover that deliberation is carried out by neurons is no more a threat to freedom than to discover that digestion is carried out by enzymes is a threat to nourishment.

What the experiments most plausibly show, then, is not that we are puppets but that our ordinary self-understanding is partly mistaken about how choosing works. It is a long way from the conclusion that choosing does not exist.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central thesis of the passage?

options.A: Laboratory studies of the readiness potential have conclusively shown that conscious deliberation plays no causal role in any human action.
options.B: Compatibilism is the only defensible account of free will because every other account is refuted by timing studies of the brain.
options.C: Neuroscientific findings correct a mistaken picture of how choosing works but fall well short of showing that choosing is an illusion.
options.D: Philosophers who defend free will should abandon their position because introspective reports of decision timing cannot be trusted at all.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage ends by saying the experiments show a partly mistaken self-understanding, not that choosing does not exist. Why the others are wrong: A) Overstates the passage; the author denies the experiments show this. B) The author favors compatibilism but does not claim it is the only defensible view or that timing studies refute rivals. D) The author questions timing reports but does not tell philosophers to abandon their position.
questions.trap: Choosing the answer that takes the experiment's popular conclusion as the author's own.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of averaging a signal aligned to the movement serves primarily to

options.A: demonstrate that the readiness potential is absent when volunteers make a deliberate choice instead of responding to a spontaneous urge.
options.B: show that the clock-hand method of timing awareness is less accurate than methods based on electrical recordings from the scalp.
options.C: argue that random neural fluctuations are unrelated to the production of movement and can safely be ignored by researchers.
options.D: suggest that the apparent early ramp may be an artifact of how the data are processed rather than a marker of decision.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The averaging point supports the claim that a ramp can be manufactured from noise selected backward from movement. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage never says the signal disappears for deliberate choices. B) The clock-hand issue is discussed separately and is not compared with electrical methods here. C) The passage says noise makes movement more likely, so it is not unrelated.
questions.trap: Confusing the first objection (what the signal means) with the second (timing of awareness).

questions.stem: The author's treatment of the third part of the argument assumes which of the following?

options.A: Any decision that is made after extended deliberation must be free, regardless of how its neural preparation is organized.
options.B: Participants in laboratory studies are generally unable to follow instructions about when to move or when to report awareness.
options.C: The significance of a decision for a person's life determines how quickly the corresponding brain activity begins.
options.D: Arbitrary flicks of the wrist and long deliberation about a career may involve different kinds of decision processes.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says generalizing from capricious flicks assumes all decisions are of one kind, which must be shown. Why the others are wrong: A) The author claims only that deliberation has not been shown ineffective, not that it must be free. B) Nothing suggests participants cannot follow instructions. C) The passage makes no claim about timing of brain activity relative to stakes.
questions.trap: Reading the author's caution as a positive claim that deliberate choices are free.

questions.stem: Suppose later studies found that brain signals reliably predicted, many seconds in advance, which job offer people would accept after weeks of deliberation. How would this finding bear on the passage?

options.A: It would confirm the author's view that the readiness potential is nothing more than averaged random neural fluctuation.
options.B: It would show that compatibilists are wrong to define freedom in terms of responsiveness to reasons and revision of one's course.
options.C: It would weaken the author's objection that results from arbitrary tasks cannot be extended to weighty, deliberate choices.
options.D: It would be irrelevant, because the author holds that evidence about the brain can never bear on questions about free will.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The third objection says arbitrary-task data do not speak to deliberation; such a finding would supply data on deliberation. Why the others are wrong: A) The finding concerns prediction of weighty choices, not the noise account of the ramp. B) Prediction alone does not show reasons-responsiveness is absent, so compatibilism is not refuted. D) The author explicitly says neuroscience is not irrelevant.
questions.trap: Treating any neural predictability as automatically refuting compatibilism.

questions.stem: The comparison of digestion and enzymes to deliberation and neurons is intended to illustrate that

options.A: discovering the physical basis of a process does not by itself show that the process fails to do what it appears to do.
options.B: deliberation and digestion are equally automatic processes that occur largely outside conscious awareness and voluntary control.
options.C: neurons and enzymes are the only components in the body whose activity is relevant to philosophical questions about agency.
options.D: compatibilists believe that freedom and nourishment are both illusions that science will eventually be able to explain away.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The analogy shows that a mechanism underlying a function does not threaten the function. Why the others are wrong: B) The analogy is about mechanism and function, not automaticity. C) No claim of exclusivity is made. D) Compatibilists are said to defend freedom, not call it an illusion.
questions.trap: Taking the analogy to claim that deliberation is as automatic as digestion.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims would the author be most likely to accept?

options.A: Evidence that unconscious processes determine which options come to mind counts against the command-post picture of the self.
options.B: Evidence that consciousness arrives late would prove that people are not responsible for the consequences of their choices.
options.C: Evidence from timing studies is the best available basis for deciding whether deliberation is causally effective in daily life.
options.D: Evidence that decisions have neural causes would leave the command-post picture entirely untouched while harming compatibilism.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says such evidence damages the command-post picture, though only a particular version of the picture. Why the others are wrong: B) The author never links late consciousness to loss of responsibility. C) The author says such studies do not speak directly to deliberation. D) The author says the evidence does damage the picture and not compatibilism.
questions.trap: Overreaching from late awareness to claims about moral responsibility.

passages.passage_text:
The phrase "Silk Road" suggests a single highway along which caravans carried bolts of cloth from China to Rome. The image is vivid and misleading. The term itself was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, and it entered popular usage only in the twentieth century. No ancient traveler would have recognized it. What existed instead was a shifting web of routes across deserts, mountain passes, steppe, and sea lanes, and almost nobody traveled its whole length. Goods moved in relays, passing through the hands of many intermediaries, each of whom took a margin and each of whom shaped what was passed on.

This relay structure matters for the question of what, exactly, was exchanged. Silk was certainly traded, and it was prized in distant courts, but it was far from the only commodity, and for much of the period it was not the most important one. Horses from Central Asia were of intense strategic interest to Chinese dynasties, which paid for them in textiles. Glassware, spices, gold, incense, medicinal plants, and precious stones moved in several directions. Bulky goods rarely traveled far overland, since the cost of transport quickly exceeded their value, which is why the overland trade favored items of high value and low weight. Much of the exchange of heavier goods took place by sea, a fact that the overland metaphor tends to conceal.

If goods were only part of the story, ideas and techniques were arguably the larger part. Buddhism traveled from northern India across Central Asia into China, changing as it went and absorbing local forms of art and ritual. Manichaean, Christian, and later Islamic communities followed similar paths. Papermaking spread westward over several centuries, eventually transforming record-keeping and scholarship in the Islamic world and Europe. Crops, instruments, and mathematical methods traveled alongside. Disease traveled too, and the diffusion of plague along trading routes is one of the sharper reminders that connection has costs as well as benefits.

The people who carried these things were not passive conduits. Merchants from Sogdiana, in what is now Uzbekistan, acted for centuries as brokers between cultures, writing in their own language, founding communities in Chinese cities, and translating religious texts. Historians who read the exchange as a contest between two great empires miss the contribution of smaller societies in the middle. Oasis towns have yielded documents in a half-dozen languages recording contracts, loans, and letters concerning ordinary business.

Skeptics argue that the romantic story has been inflated by modern interest. Governments now promote the idea for diplomatic and commercial reasons, and the label is attached to initiatives that bear little relation to the historical record. There is some justice in the complaint, but it should not be pushed too far. That the name is a modern invention does not show that the phenomenon was imaginary, any more than the coining of the word "Renaissance" long after the fact shows that nothing changed in fifteenth-century Italy. The more reasonable conclusion is that the metaphor of a road should be replaced by something more accurate, such as a network or an ecology of exchange, and that the importance of the connections should be assessed by their consequences instead of by the glamour of their name.

The lesson, then, is about method as much as about trade. Historians should be wary of metaphors that make complicated processes look tidy. A road implies a beginning and an end, a direction, a traveler. A network implies none of these, and the history it describes is better for the lack.

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

options.A: argue that overland trade across Eurasia was economically insignificant compared with the exchange of goods carried by sea.
options.B: replace a misleading metaphor with a more accurate account of how goods, ideas, and diseases moved across Eurasia.
options.C: defend the traditional picture of the Silk Road against modern skeptics who regard it as a diplomatic invention.
options.D: demonstrate that Chinese dynasties dominated long-distance exchange and that smaller societies played only a supporting role.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage corrects the road metaphor and argues for a network picture while describing what moved. Why the others are wrong: A) Sea trade is mentioned as underrepresented, but the passage does not call overland trade insignificant. C) The author partly agrees with skeptics and proposes revising, not defending, the traditional picture. D) The author stresses the role of smaller societies such as Sogdiana.
questions.trap: Seizing on one detail (sea trade or skeptics) rather than the overall aim.

questions.stem: According to the passage, overland trade favored items of high value and low weight because

options.A: rulers along the routes imposed heavy taxes on bulky goods but allowed lightweight luxuries to pass without any duties.
options.B: merchants in oasis towns refused to handle goods that could not be carried by a single traveler from end to end.
options.C: the expense of moving bulky goods over long distances by land would soon exceed what they were worth.
options.D: demand for heavy goods such as grain and timber was lower in China than demand for textiles and horses.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage states transport cost quickly exceeded the value of bulky goods. Why the others are wrong: A) No taxation is mentioned. B) Goods moved in relays, not by a single traveler. D) The passage gives no comparison of demand for heavy goods.
questions.trap: Importing a plausible-sounding economic reason not given in the text.

questions.stem: The reference to the coining of the word "Renaissance" most nearly serves to

options.A: suggest that fifteenth-century Italy was more closely connected to Asian trade networks than historians have acknowledged.
options.B: illustrate how governments use historical labels to promote contemporary diplomatic and commercial initiatives abroad.
options.C: indicate that most historical periods are named by writers who had little knowledge of the events they described.
options.D: show that a name invented after the fact does not prove that the thing it names never happened.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The analogy answers the skeptics: late coinage of a term does not make the phenomenon imaginary. Why the others are wrong: A) The analogy is not about Italian links with Asia. B) Government promotion is a separate point. C) The passage makes no claim about writers' knowledge.
questions.trap: Missing that the example is an analogy about naming, not about Italy.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the exchange of ideas and techniques was arguably the larger part of the story?

options.A: Documents from oasis towns showing that contracts and loans were written in several different languages by local traders.
options.B: Archaeological evidence that almost all religious and technical change in China was homegrown and predated contact.
options.C: Evidence that Sogdian merchants founded settlements in Chinese cities and translated religious texts into local languages.
options.D: Records showing that horses from Central Asia were purchased by Chinese dynasties in exchange for large quantities of textiles.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Evidence that borrowed ideas and techniques were largely not borrowed would undercut the claim. Why the others are wrong: A) Multilingual documents support the importance of cultural intermediaries. C) Translation and settlement support the idea-exchange claim. D) Horse-for-textile trade concerns goods, and does not bear on the ideas claim.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about goods that merely seems related instead of evidence that contradicts the claim.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the "contest between two great empires" reading of Eurasian exchange is flawed because it

options.A: overlooks intermediary societies that acted as brokers, translators, and settlers between the larger powers.
options.B: exaggerates the amount of silk that reached the Roman world relative to the amount of glassware and incense.
options.C: assumes that Buddhism spread to China through military conquest and not through the movement of merchants.
options.D: relies on documents from oasis towns that the author considers too unreliable to support firm conclusions.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The Sogdian example shows smaller societies in the middle were significant. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage does not tie the flaw to silk quantities. C) Conquest is never mentioned as the assumed route of Buddhism. D) The author calls oasis documents rich evidence.
questions.trap: Attributing to the text claims about conquest or document unreliability.

questions.stem: The author's concluding statement that the history described by a network is "better for the lack" of a beginning, end, and traveler implies that

options.A: an accurate account of this exchange has to describe many interacting participants and directions, not one journey.
options.B: historians of trade should avoid describing individual merchants and focus only on large impersonal economic forces.
options.C: the Silk Road never had any identifiable starting points such as cities, ports, or mountain passes along its routes.
options.D: metaphors should be avoided in historical writing altogether because they cannot represent complicated processes.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The network image is preferred because the real process lacked a single direction or traveler. Why the others are wrong: B) The author praises Sogdian merchants as agents. C) The author names oasis towns and routes, so identifiable places existed. D) The author recommends a better metaphor, not abandoning metaphor.
questions.trap: Over-generalizing a warning about one metaphor to all metaphors.

passages.passage_text:
When Michel de Montaigne retired to his tower in the 1570s and began writing short, wandering prose pieces about cannibals, thumbs, idleness, and friendship, he called them essais, a word meaning trials or attempts. The name was a statement of method. A treatise advances from definitions to conclusions and expects the reader to accept both. Montaigne offered something less secure: a mind testing a question against its own experience, reporting what happened, and frequently ending where it had not expected to be. The essay has been defined ever since by this refusal to pretend that thought arrives finished.

That provisional quality is easily mistaken for a lack of rigor. Defenders of the treatise tradition have complained that the essay permits writers to evade the burden of proof. An essayist may digress, change his mind, or leave a question open, and no one can say he has broken a rule. But the criticism assumes that the only rigor worth having is the rigor of deduction. A good essay has another kind: fidelity to the way a question actually looks from a particular position, with its complications left in. Montaigne's reflections on cruelty, for example, are persuasive precisely because he admits his own squeamishness and then reasons from it, rather than hiding it behind an abstract principle. The essay's discipline lies in honesty about the process.

The form also has a distinctive relation to its reader. The treatise addresses a student who must be instructed; the essay addresses a companion who is invited to watch someone think. This explains why the great essayists are so often remembered as voices and not as systems. We read Johnson, Hazlitt, Woolf, and Baldwin partly for what they say and partly for the company of the sensibility saying it. The personal essay in particular depends on a calculated intimacy, one in which the writer discloses enough to be believed and withholds enough to avoid self-absorption. When that balance fails, the result is confession without insight, the self displayed rather than used.

It is tempting to conclude that the essay is therefore a purely literary form, unconcerned with knowledge. That would be a mistake. The essay has been a vehicle for serious intellectual work, from Bacon's compressed advice on statecraft to modern writing on science and law. Its advantage in such domains is that it can hold together considerations that systematic argument must separate. A treatise on grief must choose a definition of grief; an essay can follow a loss through memory, ritual, and embarrassment without deciding in advance which of these is the real subject. What it offers is not a conclusion that can be cited but an understanding that must be experienced.

The present danger to the form is less its critics than its imitators. The commercial appetite for opinion has produced a great deal of writing that borrows the essay's first-person voice while abandoning its method. The opinion column begins with a conclusion and recruits experience as decoration. The reader learns what the author thinks but never watches the thinking happen. In a genuine essay the conclusion is a discovery, however modest, and the reader can tell. Where the writer already knows what he will find, the trial is a performance, and the word has lost its meaning.

Montaigne's own motto, which he is said to have kept inscribed in his library, was a question: what do I know? The essay, at its best, keeps that question open without making it an excuse for saying nothing.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?

options.A: A chronological history of the essay from Montaigne to the present, with each period's major writers evaluated in turn.
options.B: A comparison of the treatise and the essay concluding that the treatise is more rigorous but less pleasant to read.
options.C: A defense of Montaigne's reputation followed by a series of examples of modern essayists who surpass his achievements.
options.D: A statement of the form's method, replies to objections, remarks on reader and scope, and a warning about imitation.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage defines the form, answers the charge of laxity, discusses reader and scope, then warns about opinion writing. Why the others are wrong: A) The structure is thematic, not chronological. B) The author does not conclude the treatise is more rigorous. C) Montaigne is not said to be surpassed.
questions.trap: Reading the passage as a historical survey because it begins with Montaigne.

questions.stem: The author's response to the charge that the essay evades the burden of proof is that

options.A: the essay does not have to meet any standard of rigor because its purpose is literary pleasure rather than knowledge.
options.B: the essay has its own kind of rigor, which lies in honestly reporting how a question appears from a given position.
options.C: most essays are in fact organized as deductive arguments, although their digressions can make this difficult to notice.
options.D: the burden of proof is lighter in domains such as statecraft and law than it is in the natural sciences.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author claims a different rigor: fidelity to how a question looks, complications included. Why the others are wrong: A) The author rejects the idea that the essay is purely literary and unconcerned with knowledge. C) The author says the essay does not proceed by deduction. D) No comparison with the natural sciences is drawn.
questions.trap: Choosing the concession that the essay is exempt from standards.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the personal essay fails when the writer

options.A: withholds so much personal experience that the reader cannot tell what the writer's position on the question is.
options.B: discloses so much of the self that nothing is learned from the disclosure about the question under discussion.
options.C: borrows the first-person voice from earlier essayists instead of developing a style that reflects an individual sensibility.
options.D: reaches a conclusion that the reader finds modest or unexpected at the end of a long and wandering chain of thought.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Failure is 'confession without insight, the self displayed rather than used.' Why the others are wrong: A) Withholding too much is not described as the failure; self-absorption is. C) Imitation of voice is attributed to opinion writing, not to this failure. D) Modest or unexpected conclusions are praised, not criticized.
questions.trap: Reversing the balance the author describes between disclosure and withholding.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an opinion column differs from a genuine essay in that the column

options.A: treats the author's experience as support for a conclusion already reached, instead of as material for discovery.
options.B: avoids the first-person voice and presents its claims as though they were established by impersonal methods.
options.C: addresses a student who must be instructed rather than a companion who is invited to watch someone think.
options.D: leaves its central question open and therefore cannot offer readers any understanding of the topic discussed.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The column 'begins with a conclusion and recruits experience as decoration.' Why the others are wrong: B) The column borrows the first-person voice. C) That contrast describes the treatise, not the column. D) Leaving questions open is characteristic of the essay.
questions.trap: Confusing the opinion column with the treatise.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that the essay can handle considerations that systematic argument must separate?

options.A: A survey showing that most readers can name more essayists than they can name authors of philosophical treatises.
options.B: A history showing that Bacon wrote his essays after completing longer and more systematic works on the same subjects.
options.C: An analysis showing that modern opinion columns are more widely read than the essays of Johnson, Hazlitt, or Woolf.
options.D: A study in which readers of essays about bereavement reported grasping aspects of grief that definitions had left out.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Evidence that essays convey aspects of a subject that definitions miss directly supports the claim. Why the others are wrong: A) Name recognition does not bear on cognitive range. B) Bacon's order of composition is irrelevant to the claim. C) Popularity of columns does not address the essay's capabilities.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about popularity rather than about what the form can accomplish.

questions.stem: The reference to Montaigne's motto in the final paragraph primarily serves to

options.A: suggest that Montaigne himself doubted that any essay could succeed in producing knowledge about human nature.
options.B: show that the form was invented as a response to the scholarly skepticism that dominated sixteenth-century libraries.
options.C: support the claim that a writer who asks a question cannot also be said to have reached a conclusion of any kind.
options.D: illustrate that the essay's commitment to inquiry is compatible with leaving questions unresolved.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The motto is a question kept open, matching the author's final sentence about the essay not using openness as an excuse. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the essay can yield understanding, so doubt about knowledge is not implied. B) No historical claim about scholarly skepticism is made. C) The author says conclusions in essays are discoveries, so questions and conclusions can coexist.
questions.trap: Equating an open question with complete skepticism.

passages.passage_text:
The modern public museum presents itself as a neutral custodian: a place where objects of lasting value are kept safe, arranged sensibly, and shown to anyone who walks in. Few institutions have been so thoroughly shaped by the circumstances of their founding. The ancestors of the museum were private cabinets of curiosities, assembled by princes and scholars in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, in which fossils, coins, instruments, and exotic artifacts were displayed together as evidence of the collector's reach. The institution acquired its public character only later, most dramatically when revolutionary France converted royal and church property into a national collection open to citizens. From the start, then, the museum was bound up with questions of who owns the past and for whom it is displayed.

This history complicates the claim of neutrality. To collect is to select, and to display is to arrange; every gallery embodies a judgment about what belongs together and what deserves a room of its own. Nineteenth-century museums frequently sorted human cultures on a scale of progress, placing European art at the summit and the artifacts of colonized peoples in the category of ethnography. Visitors who passed from one wing to another were being taught a theory, though the theory was rarely stated.

Critics have drawn from this a severe conclusion: that museums are instruments of power whose authority rests on concealment. The argument has force in particular cases. Many celebrated collections were assembled through conquest, coercive purchase, or the removal of objects from communities that did not consent. But the severe conclusion overreaches when it treats the museum's origins as a complete account of its function. Institutions are not prisoners of their beginnings. The public art gallery that began as a display of royal wealth has become, in many cities, one of the few spaces where people of different backgrounds meet in the presence of the same objects.

A more useful response is to ask what a museum can honestly claim to do. It cannot claim to present the past as it was, for the past does not arrive in glass cases. What it can do is preserve material that would otherwise be lost, make that material accessible, and offer interpretations that are open to challenge. The third of these is the one that most needs emphasis. A label that says "Greek, fifth century" invites the visitor to treat the object as a fact, whereas a label that says how the piece was acquired, what is uncertain about its dating, and why curators have placed it beside its neighbors invites the visitor to treat the display as an argument. The latter does not make the museum less authoritative. It moves the source of authority from the building to the quality of the reasons offered.

Some curators fear that such candor will erode public confidence. The evidence suggests the opposite risk. Trust that depends on visitors not knowing how collections were formed is fragile, and it is likely to collapse when the facts become known, as they increasingly do. Trust that rests on a record of acknowledging uncertainty and correcting error is sturdier, since it was never staked on perfection. Scientific institutions have found this to be true, and there is no reason to think museums are different.

The museum is therefore best understood neither as a temple of neutral value nor as a mere apparatus of domination, but as an institution that makes claims and ought to be held accountable for them. That standard is more demanding than neutrality, and it is also more honest.

questions.stem: The main idea of the passage is that museums

options.A: are fundamentally instruments of power whose collections cannot be justified in light of the circumstances under which they were assembled.
options.B: have succeeded in becoming neutral custodians of the past by moving away from their origins in private collections.
options.C: should be understood as interpretive institutions whose authority depends on the reasons they offer, not on a claim of neutrality.
options.D: should reduce public confidence in their holdings by emphasizing how much of the historical record remains uncertain.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The final paragraph presents the museum as an institution that makes claims and should be accountable for them. Why the others are wrong: A) The author rejects the severe conclusion as overreaching. B) The author denies that neutrality is an accurate description. D) The author argues candor strengthens, not reduces, trust.
questions.trap: Taking the critics' severe view as the author's own.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that nineteenth-century museums taught visitors a theory primarily through

options.A: explicit labels that stated the supposed scale of progress and explained where each culture belonged on it.
options.B: the physical arrangement of objects, which put European art and colonized peoples' artifacts in separate categories.
options.C: public lectures delivered by curators who defended the hierarchy of cultures in front of the collections.
options.D: the removal of objects from communities, which showed visitors that some cultures were unfit to keep their heritage.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says the theory was 'rarely stated' and conveyed by how the wings were arranged. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the theory was rarely stated. C) Lectures are not mentioned. D) The removal of objects is discussed separately and is not said to teach this theory.
questions.trap: Assuming a theory must be taught through explicit statement.

questions.stem: The author mentions the public art gallery that began as a display of royal wealth in order to

options.A: show that an institution's present function cannot be inferred from the conditions of its origin alone.
options.B: prove that the claim of neutrality is justified because many cities now have galleries open to all citizens.
options.C: argue that private collections have always been more beneficial to the public than institutions founded by states.
options.D: support the claim that revolutionary governments were more concerned with public access than earlier collectors.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The example supports the claim that institutions are not prisoners of their beginnings. Why the others are wrong: B) The author denies neutrality; the example concerns function, not neutrality. C) No comparison of private and state collections is made. D) The example is not about revolutionary governments' motives.
questions.trap: Interpreting a point about change over time as endorsement of neutrality.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the kind of label the author would prefer?

options.A: A card stating the culture and century of a vase and its measurements, with no additional commentary that might distract viewers.
options.B: A card describing a vase as one of the finest examples of its type and praising the skill of the craftsperson who made it.
options.C: A card noting that a vase was purchased from a dealer in 1890, that its date is disputed, and why it hangs beside two other works.
options.D: A card asking visitors to decide for themselves what a vase means, with no information about its origin or acquisition.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The preferred label discloses acquisition, uncertainty, and curatorial reasoning. Why the others are wrong: A) This resembles the 'Greek, fifth century' label the author criticizes. B) Praise offers no reasons open to challenge. D) The author wants offered reasons, not their absence.
questions.trap: Mistaking minimal information for neutrality.

questions.stem: The author's argument about public trust is based on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Visitors place greater trust in museums that avoid discussing their history of acquiring objects through conquest.
options.B: Scientific institutions have generally avoided admitting uncertainty because doing so reduces public confidence in results.
options.C: Information about how collections were formed is likely to become widely known over time.
options.D: Curators who fear a loss of confidence are mistaken about how many people actually visit museums.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Trust built on ignorance collapses 'when the facts become known, as they increasingly do.' Why the others are wrong: A) The author argues the opposite about concealment. B) The author says scientific institutions confirm that acknowledging uncertainty builds trust. D) Visitor numbers are not at issue.
questions.trap: Reading a fear the author rejects as a premise of the argument.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most undermine the author's claim that a museum's origins do not fully determine its function?

options.A: Evidence that some museums have returned objects to communities from which they were removed in earlier centuries.
options.B: Evidence that visitors to old galleries consistently describe them as expressions of the culture that founded them.
options.C: Evidence that visitors from different backgrounds meet in public galleries more often than in other civic spaces.
options.D: Evidence that cabinets of curiosities included fossils and instruments in addition to coins and artifacts.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) If visitors consistently see galleries as expressions of the founding culture, origins would still be driving function, contrary to the claim. Why the others are wrong: A) Returns show institutions changing, supporting the claim. C) Diverse meeting supports the claim. D) The contents of cabinets are irrelevant.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about change that actually supports the author.

passages.passage_text:
Few art forms have been so closely identified with the idea of a nation as opera. Textbooks routinely present Giuseppe Verdi as the musical voice of Italian unification, Richard Wagner as the embodiment of German cultural aspiration, and Bedrich Smetana as the founder of a Czech national style. The pattern seems to confirm a simple thesis: a people discovers its identity, and its composers give that identity sound. Yet a closer look at how particular works came to be regarded as national suggests that the relation between music and nation runs largely in the opposite direction. Nations, or at least their mythologies, are often assembled from music, and the assembling is done not by composers but by audiences, critics, and later historians.

Consider the best-known case. The chorus of Hebrew slaves in Verdi's early opera Nabucco, sung in the 1840s, is often said to have been taken up on the spot by Italian patriots as an anthem of resistance to Austrian rule. The story is stirring, and much of it appears to have been added in later decades, when Verdi had become a national monument and the unification movement had victory to commemorate. Contemporary reports show enthusiastic audiences, but the political meaning of that enthusiasm was uncertain, and the opera's biblical subject matter was not obviously a coded message. The legend tells us less about what happened in a Milan theater in 1842 than about what Italians later needed to remember.

This does not mean that opera played no role in nation-building. It means that the role was subtler than the legend suggests. Opera was a public art, performed in cities where the educated classes gathered, and its choice of language mattered. In regions where the language of the ruling court differed from the language of the people, composing an opera in the vernacular was itself a political act, since it asserted that the local tongue was fit for the grandest of forms. Smetana's operas, written in Czech for a theater built partly by public subscription, are a better example of this than anything in Verdi, and their significance is institutional as much as musical: they gave an audience a reason to gather and to see itself gathering.

There is a further complication. The characteristics that listeners most readily call national are not stable. A folk-like melody, a dance rhythm, or an orchestral color that seems quintessentially Czech or Russian was frequently borrowed from elsewhere or invented to meet a market that expected exoticism. The result is a feedback loop: audiences abroad identify a sound as typical of a country, composers at home reinforce it, and over time the sound comes to seem an ancient inheritance.

None of this diminishes the works themselves. A listener moved by the exiles' chorus does not need to believe in the legend to be moved, and a composer who draws on local idioms may do so out of sincere attachment. But a historian should be careful not to treat the stories that nations tell about their art as evidence of how that art was first heard. The relation between opera and national identity is better described as a long negotiation than as a simple expression, and its history is full of retrospective revision.

What emerges, in short, is a reminder that cultural memory edits the past in favor of a satisfying plot. Opera did not simply reflect nations; it supplied the occasions, the language, and the stories from which they learned to imagine themselves.

questions.stem: The author's primary claim about the relation between opera and national identity is that

options.A: composers of the nineteenth century were generally indifferent to politics and wrote operas solely for commercial success.
options.B: national meanings attributed to operas were often built by later audiences and historians, not expressed by the works at first.
options.C: opera had no meaningful influence on the development of national consciousness in countries that were ruled by foreign courts.
options.D: the national character of an opera can be determined by identifying folk melodies that the composer borrowed from local traditions.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The opening says the relation runs largely in the opposite direction, with audiences and later historians assembling national meaning. Why the others are wrong: A) The author grants that composers could be sincere in drawing on local idioms and that opera did play a role. C) The author says opera did play a role, especially vernacular opera. D) The passage argues such 'national' melodies were often borrowed or invented.
questions.trap: Treating a revisionist argument as a denial of any role for opera.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Nabucco legend

options.A: probably grew later, when Verdi was a national monument and the unification movement could celebrate success.
options.B: was invented by Austrian officials who wished to portray Italian patriots as threats to public order in Milan.
options.C: is entirely false, because contemporary reports show that early audiences were indifferent to the chorus of slaves.
options.D: is supported by the opera's biblical subject matter, which was widely understood as a coded message of resistance.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says much of the story seems to have been added later, when commemoration was needed. Why the others are wrong: B) Austrian invention is not mentioned. C) Contemporary reports show enthusiastic audiences, so the passage does not call everything false. D) The author says the subject matter was not obviously a coded message.
questions.trap: Overcorrecting from 'partly legendary' to 'entirely false.'

questions.stem: The author regards Smetana's operas as a better example of nation-building than Verdi's because Smetana's operas

options.A: contained more melodies derived from authentic Czech folk traditions than Verdi's work did from Italian sources.
options.B: were performed more frequently in foreign theaters, where audiences were eager to hear a distinctly national sound.
options.C: expressed political aspirations more explicitly than Verdi's work, which was concerned mainly with biblical subjects.
options.D: were sung in the vernacular and gave audiences an institution in which to gather and see themselves doing so.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The significance is described as institutional: Czech language, public subscription, and gathering. Why the others are wrong: A) The author suggests national melodies are unreliable, and makes no claim of more authentic folk material. B) Foreign demand is cited as part of the feedback loop, not as Smetana's advantage. C) The author does not claim Smetana's works were more explicit politically.
questions.trap: Equating national significance with folk content.

questions.stem: The 'feedback loop' described in the fourth paragraph refers to a process in which

options.A: composers at home borrow melodies from foreign sources, which then persuade audiences abroad that the melodies are original.
options.B: critics who write about national style are influenced by composers' statements, which in turn depend on critics' earlier judgments.
options.C: foreign listeners label a sound as typical, composers at home reinforce it, and the sound later appears to be an ancient inheritance.
options.D: audiences at home demand exotic sounds from composers who learn to avoid anything that would remind listeners of foreign music.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The paragraph describes foreign identification, home reinforcement, and later perception of antiquity. Why the others are wrong: A) Borrowing is mentioned but the loop is not about persuading foreigners of originality. B) Critics' statements are not part of this loop. D) The loop concerns foreign audiences' expectations, not audiences at home avoiding foreign sounds.
questions.trap: Garbling the direction of influence between audiences abroad and composers at home.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims is most consistent with the author's view of cultural memory?

options.A: Legends about works of art are usually reliable because they were preserved by people who had direct experience of events.
options.B: Stories communities tell about their art may reveal more about later needs than about early reception.
options.C: Cultural memory is less reliable for music than for literature because music cannot be preserved in written records.
options.D: Listeners who are moved by a work should abandon any belief in legends associated with it in order to appreciate it.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says the legend reveals what Italians later needed to remember. Why the others are wrong: A) The author doubts such legends. C) No comparison of music with literature is made. D) The author says one need not believe the legend to be moved, but does not require abandoning it.
questions.trap: Choosing a claim stronger than the one the author endorses.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most weaken the author's account of the Nabucco legend?

options.A: Theater records showing that Nabucco was performed to full houses in Milan during its first season and in later revivals.
options.B: Letters from Verdi's contemporaries describing the music of the slaves' chorus as unusually moving and memorable to listeners.
options.C: Newspaper reports from 1842 showing that audiences explicitly linked the chorus to Austrian rule and demanded it be repeated as a protest.
options.D: Evidence that Verdi was honored as a national figure only after unification, when the movement had succeeded in its aims.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Contemporary evidence of explicit political reading would undermine the claim that the political meaning was added later. Why the others are wrong: A) Full houses fit the passage's report of enthusiastic but politically uncertain audiences. B) Praise of the music does not bear on political meaning. D) This agrees with the author's claim that the legend grew after Verdi became a monument.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence of popularity, which the author already accepts.

passages.passage_text:
Anyone who has called a father's brother and a mother's brother by the same word, uncle, has taken part in a system of kinship classification without noticing. English speakers group together a surprisingly diverse set of relatives under a handful of terms, and the grouping seems so natural that it takes effort to see it as a choice. Other languages divide the same relatives differently. In some, a father's brother is called by the same word as the father, while a mother's brother has a separate term. In others, all cousins are called by sibling terms, or a mother's sister is addressed as mother. The study of such systems was among the earliest projects of anthropology, and it has yielded two lessons that pull in opposite directions.

The first lesson, associated with the nineteenth-century American lawyer and ethnologist Lewis Henry Morgan, was that terminology is a window onto social organization. Morgan collected vocabularies from dozens of societies and found that they fell into a small number of types, which later scholars named after the peoples who exemplified them, such as Hawaiian, Iroquois, Omaha, and Eskimo. The tidy variety of types seemed to demand explanation, and the explanation most readily available was that each system reflected the way a society organized descent, marriage, and inheritance. If a father's brother is called father, perhaps it is because he shares the father's rights and duties toward the child. The terms, on this view, are compressed rules.

This hypothesis has had notable successes. In societies that trace descent through one parent's line, the terms often do distinguish relatives on the side of descent from those outside it, and these distinctions correspond to rules about whom one may marry or from whom one may inherit. The pattern is statistically real even where individual cases deviate from it. Terminology, then, is not arbitrary. But the hypothesis has also been pressed too far. Systems of the same type turn up among societies with very different institutions, and societies with similar institutions sometimes use unlike systems. A vocabulary can outlast the arrangements that produced it, much as English retains spellings that no longer correspond to pronunciation.

The second lesson, which emerged in the twentieth century, was more skeptical. The American anthropologist David Schneider argued that scholars had assumed too readily that kinship is grounded in biological reproduction and that other cultures simply classify the same biological facts in different ways. In many societies, he observed, relatedness is created by sharing food, living in the same house, or exchanging care, and it can be dissolved as well as created. To treat a term as a classification of genealogical positions is to import the questioner's assumptions. If the terms do not map biology in the first place, a theory that explains deviations from a biological map has the wrong problem.

Reconciling the two lessons is not easy, but it may not be necessary to choose between them. Morgan's insight survives in a weaker form: terms reflect, among other things, the ways a society allocates obligations, and this is a claim about practice rather than biology. Schneider's insight reminds us that what is being classified is not given in advance. A kinship term is a tool for organizing social life, and tools are shaped both by the work they do and by the hands that hold them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

options.A: Kinship terms partly reflect social organization, but early biological assumptions were challenged, and both insights matter.
options.B: Kinship terminology is arbitrary because systems of the same type appear in societies that have very different institutions.
options.C: Morgan's classification of kinship systems has been refuted by later anthropologists who showed that terms reflect only biology.
options.D: Kinship is created entirely through food sharing and cohabitation, so genealogical terms have no value for social analysis.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage presents Morgan's lesson, Schneider's lesson, and a reconciliation. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says terminology is 'not arbitrary.' C) Schneider denied that terms map biology; the author says Morgan's insight survives in weaker form. D) The author does not claim kinship is created entirely this way or that terms are valueless.
questions.trap: Adopting one lesson as the whole conclusion.

questions.stem: The comparison of kinship vocabulary to English spelling is used to illustrate that

options.A: kinship terms and spellings are both chosen deliberately by speakers who wish to reflect the structure of society.
options.B: English kinship terms are less reliable guides to social organization than the terms used in non-Western societies.
options.C: a system of terms can persist after the social arrangements that produced it have changed.
options.D: societies with similar institutions will nearly always develop similar systems of terms and similar spelling conventions.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The analogy shows vocabulary can outlast arrangements that produced it. Why the others are wrong: A) The analogy stresses persistence, not deliberate choice. B) No ranking of English against other systems is made. D) The passage says similar institutions sometimes yield unlike systems.
questions.trap: Missing the point about persistence and reading the analogy as about choice.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support Morgan's hypothesis as the passage describes it?

options.A: Societies in which a father's brother is called by the father's term also give him the father's rights over the child's marriage.
options.B: Societies using the Hawaiian type of system are found on several continents and have widely different histories of settlement.
options.C: Societies in which descent is traced through one parent's line sometimes use terms that are borrowed from neighboring peoples.
options.D: Societies in which cousins are called by sibling terms are found in regions with very different marriage customs.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) A match between a term and shared rights and duties directly fits the 'terms are compressed rules' idea. Why the others are wrong: B) That pattern would suggest the type does not depend on institutions. C) Borrowed terms would weaken the link between terms and institutions. D) This would show a term type unconnected to institutions, which cuts against the hypothesis.
questions.trap: Selecting a correlation that sounds relevant but does not support the term-rule link.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Schneider's objection to earlier kinship theory was that it

options.A: ignored the fact that most societies trace descent through only one parent's line when assigning kinship terms to relatives.
options.B: relied on vocabularies collected from too few societies to establish that terms fall into a small number of types.
options.C: treated genealogy as the universal basis of kinship, though many societies create relatedness through shared practice.
options.D: denied that terms reflect the way a society allocates obligations, rights, and duties among its members at all.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Schneider said scholars assumed kinship is grounded in biological reproduction. Why the others are wrong: A) Descent tracing is Morgan-related and not Schneider's objection. B) Sample size is not raised. D) The author says Morgan's insight survives as a claim about practice, which Schneider's critique does not deny.
questions.trap: Attributing Morgan-era issues to Schneider's critique.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage, comparing a kinship term to a tool, suggests that

options.A: terms are best analyzed by listing the biological relationships that each of them would be used to classify.
options.B: terms are interchangeable across cultures because tools of the same type serve the same purposes everywhere.
options.C: terms were invented by anthropologists as instruments for organizing information about societies they studied.
options.D: terms are shaped by the social functions they serve and by the assumptions of the people who use and study them.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The tool image points to both function ('work it does') and the users ('hands that hold them'). Why the others are wrong: A) That is the assumption Schneider criticized. B) The passage emphasizes differences between systems. C) The terms belong to the societies studied, not to anthropologists.
questions.trap: Treating a metaphor as a literal claim about invention.

passages.passage_text:
Economists have long maintained that markets are simply tools for allocating goods, and that tools are morally neutral. If two parties agree to an exchange and no one else is harmed, the exchange makes both better off, and to forbid it is to impose one person's preferences on another. Yet there are exchanges that most people find troubling even when both parties consent: the sale of a kidney, the purchase of a university degree, the hiring of a stand-in to wait in line for a legislative hearing. The philosophical question is whether such discomfort is mere squeamishness or a sign that some goods should not be bought and sold.

Two kinds of objection are usually offered. The first is an argument from fairness. Where people are desperately poor, a consent to sell a kidney may not be truly voluntary, and a market in organs would let the wealthy draw on the bodies of the poor. This objection does not condemn the exchange itself so much as the unequal conditions under which it occurs. Its remedy, in principle, is to correct the conditions: improve the bargaining position of the poor, and the objection fades. The second objection, an argument from corruption, is of a different order. It holds that to treat certain goods as commodities degrades them, because markets express and promote attitudes toward goods that are inappropriate to them. A friendship that is purchased is no friendship at all; a prize bought is not an honor. On this view, the problem would persist even if everyone were rich and entirely free.

The corruption argument is often dismissed as sentimental, but it contains a testable idea. Introducing payment can change the meaning of an activity and thereby change behavior. In a well-known study of a day-care center, parents who were fined for arriving late began to arrive later, apparently because the fine converted a moral obligation to the teachers into a price that could be paid like any other. Research on blood donation has suggested a similar pattern: in some settings, offering payment appears to reduce rather than increase the supply, because it recasts a gift as a transaction. These findings undermine the assumption that adding a price merely adds an incentive and leaves everything else as it was.

The difficulty, as defenders of markets point out, is that the corruption argument seems to require a prior account of what each good is for, and that account is precisely what people disagree about. Without agreement on that point, appeals to corruption look like appeals to tradition. This is a fair challenge, but it does not defeat the argument; it relocates it. If the meaning of a good determines which norms are appropriate to it, then deciding where markets belong cannot be separated from deciding what we think the good is. That is a public question, and one that economists, as economists, have no special authority to answer.

The result is that the choice is not between markets and their abolition, but between thoughtful and thoughtless extensions of market reasoning. Nothing in the objection from corruption requires hostility to markets in the great majority of cases. Most people do not believe that the exchange of shoes or bread degrades either. What it requires is attention to the cases in which payment changes the character of what is bought, and a willingness to argue openly about which cases those are. Such arguments are untidy, but the alternative, treating the question as a technical matter that economic analysis can settle, quietly decides it in favor of one answer.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in the passage is to

options.A: demonstrate that markets are morally corrupting and should be removed from the allocation of most goods in society.
options.B: show that fairness objections to markets are weaker than corruption objections because the fairness problems can be solved.
options.C: argue that where markets belong cannot be settled by economic reasoning alone and requires debate about what goods mean.
options.D: defend the economic view that voluntary exchanges are beneficial against objections based on sentiment and tradition.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The conclusion says deciding where markets belong requires public debate about what goods are. Why the others are wrong: A) The author denies hostility to markets in most cases. B) The author contrasts them but does not aim to rank their strength. D) The author challenges, not defends, the purely economic view.
questions.trap: Equating the corruption argument with a call to abolish markets.

questions.stem: The author most likely regards the fairness objection as different from the corruption objection in that the fairness objection

options.A: applies only to the sale of organs, while the corruption objection applies to every exchange of goods and services.
options.B: rests on a prediction about behavior that can be tested, while the corruption objection depends only on sentiment.
options.C: could in principle be answered by improving bargaining conditions, whereas the corruption objection would remain.
options.D: depends on the claim that payment degrades the good being sold, while the corruption objection depends on inequality.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The fairness objection targets unequal conditions; the corruption objection would persist 'even if everyone were rich and entirely free.' Why the others are wrong: A) Fairness is not limited to organs and corruption does not apply to everything. B) The author says the corruption argument contains a testable idea. D) This swaps the objections' descriptions.
questions.trap: Swapping which objection concerns inequality and which concerns the meaning of goods.

questions.stem: The day-care study is used in the passage to illustrate that

options.A: fines are generally an ineffective means of enforcing rules, since parents consider them to be unjust impositions.
options.B: adding a price to an activity can change how participants understand it, and thereby alter their behavior in unexpected ways.
options.C: teachers at day-care centers are less valued by parents than workers in markets where services are sold at a price.
options.D: parents who arrive late are indifferent to the obligations that they have to teachers and other families at the center.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The fine converted a moral obligation into a price, changing behavior. Why the others are wrong: A) The study shows a specific effect on meaning, not that fines never work. C) The passage makes no claim about how parents value teachers. D) The passage says parents saw an obligation until the fine converted it.
questions.trap: Over-generalizing the study to a claim about all fines.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most weaken the author's use of research on blood donation?

options.A: A large study finding that payment increased blood donation in every setting examined, with no change in the quality of donations.
options.B: A study finding that people who donate blood without pay describe the act as meaningful and as an expression of civic duty.
options.C: A study finding that many donors would continue to give if payment were offered, though some would reduce their donations.
options.D: A study finding that paid donors were more likely to come from lower-income communities than were unpaid donors.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Uniform increases under payment would contradict the suggestion that payment can reduce supply. Why the others are wrong: B) Such descriptions are consistent with the passage. C) Mixed effects, including some reductions, are consistent with the claim that payment may reduce supply in some settings. D) This concerns fairness, not the effect of payment on supply.
questions.trap: Selecting evidence that fits the claim as 'mixed' rather than contradictory.

questions.stem: The author's response to the objection that the corruption argument requires a prior account of what goods are for is to

options.A: reject the point on the ground that all societies share a single understanding of what education and health are for.
options.B: concede the point while arguing that it shows the debate about markets to be a debate about the meaning of goods.
options.C: accept the point and conclude that appeals to corruption should therefore be set aside as appeals to tradition.
options.D: argue that economists are best qualified to settle disagreements about the purposes of the goods in question.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author calls it a fair challenge that 'relocates' the argument. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says people disagree about purposes. C) The author says the challenge does not defeat the argument. D) The author says economists have no special authority.
questions.trap: Treating a concession as a surrender of the argument.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption on which the author's final paragraph depends?

options.A: Most goods exchanged in markets, such as shoes and bread, would be degraded if they were allocated by other means.
options.B: People who object to markets on grounds of corruption are generally hostile to all forms of economic exchange.
options.C: Economic analysis of markets cannot be applied to any decision regarding the sale of organs or university degrees.
options.D: Treating market limits as a technical matter would still involve a judgment about the goods concerned.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says treating the issue as technical quietly decides it in favor of one answer. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says exchanging shoes or bread degrades neither. B) The author denies this hostility. C) The author does not say economics cannot be applied at all.
questions.trap: Choosing an extreme claim the author expressly rejects.

passages.passage_text:
Every year, millions of mice, rats, fish, and a smaller number of dogs, primates, and other animals are used in research on human and veterinary disease. Defenders of this practice appeal to its results: vaccines, anesthetics, insulin, and surgical techniques all depended on animal work. Critics reply that no benefit to humans can justify inflicting suffering on creatures that feel pain. The dispute is usually presented as a clash of moral principles, with one side counting consequences and the other insisting on limits. But the ethics of animal research turns at least as much on empirical questions as on abstract principle, and the principles themselves cannot be applied without answers to those questions.

Consider the argument from benefit. It holds that suffering inflicted on animals is justified if it is necessary to produce goods for humans that outweigh it. Whether the goods outweigh the suffering depends on how often animal experiments actually yield treatments. Some achievements, such as the development of insulin, are clear. Yet a considerable share of drugs that appear safe and effective in animals fail in human trials, often because of differences in metabolism or in the way a disease presents. If the predictive value of a model is lower than researchers claim, the benefit side of the ledger shrinks, and a moral calculation that seemed secure may not be.

The argument from rights, favored by many critics, seems to avoid empirical questions entirely. If animals have a right not to be used as mere means to others' ends, then the consequences of research are irrelevant, as they would be if the subjects were humans. But the argument faces its own empirical difficulties. It depends on the claim that the relevant features of animals, such as the capacity to suffer, are sufficiently like ours to ground similar rights, and the degree of similarity varies across species. A great deal of laboratory work involves invertebrates or fish whose capacities for experience remain uncertain, and an ethics that treats a mouse, a monkey, and a nematode alike is not easy to defend.

A framework widely adopted in research regulation tries to make progress without settling the philosophical dispute. Known as the three Rs, it asks investigators to replace animals with alternatives where possible, to reduce the number used, and to refine procedures so as to minimize distress. Its appeal is that it can be accepted by people who disagree about fundamentals: a utilitarian will welcome the reduction of suffering for the same result, and a rights theorist will welcome any movement toward abolition. Its limitation is that it can become a box-checking exercise, with committees satisfied by a gesture toward alternatives while the underlying question, whether a given experiment should be done at all, is left to a procedural default.

What follows is not that the moral questions are unimportant but that they cannot be answered in isolation from the facts. A scientist who uses animals bears a responsibility to show that the work is likely to produce knowledge that could not be obtained otherwise, and that the design is good enough for its results to mean something. A badly designed study that wastes animals is wrong on every account of the matter, however much one sympathizes with the goals of research. The most defensible position is probably neither that animal research is always justified nor that it is never so, but that each use must earn its justification through evidence the public can examine.

questions.stem: The main argument of the passage is that the ethics of animal research

options.A: is best resolved by adopting a rights-based approach that disregards the consequences of experiments for human health.
options.B: has been settled by regulatory frameworks that allow people with different philosophical views to reach agreement.
options.C: should be governed by the benefits of research, since evidence shows that animal models reliably predict human outcomes.
options.D: cannot be resolved by moral principle alone, because the principles depend on empirical claims that require evidence.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The introduction and conclusion say the ethics turns on empirical questions as well as principle. Why the others are wrong: A) The author finds rights arguments to have empirical difficulties and does not endorse them. B) The author says the three Rs can become box-checking and leave the underlying question open. C) The author says predictive value may be lower than claimed.
questions.trap: Reading a mixed position as an endorsement of one side.

questions.stem: The author mentions that many drugs that appear safe in animals fail in human trials in order to

options.A: prove that no animal research has ever contributed to the development of effective treatments for human diseases.
options.B: cast doubt on the premise that animal experiments dependably produce benefits that outweigh suffering.
options.C: support the rights-based claim that animals should not be used as means to the ends of others.
options.D: show that human trials are more ethically defensible than animal experiments because humans can give their consent.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Poor prediction shrinks the benefit side of the ledger. Why the others are wrong: A) The author cites insulin as a clear success. C) This point is about benefit, not rights. D) Consent is not discussed.
questions.trap: Over-reading a challenge to the benefit premise as total rejection.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the argument from rights depends on an empirical claim that

options.A: research on animals rarely produces results that can be applied to the treatment of human patients.
options.B: most research animals are vertebrates whose capacity for experience has been established beyond reasonable doubt.
options.C: the number of animals used each year is large enough to constitute a serious violation of their interests.
options.D: the features of animals that ground rights, such as capacity to suffer, are sufficiently similar to ours.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says the argument depends on similarity of relevant capacities to ours. Why the others are wrong: A) That claim belongs to the benefit argument. B) The author says capacities for fish and invertebrates are uncertain. C) Numbers are not offered as the empirical basis of the rights argument.
questions.trap: Mixing premises of the benefit argument with those of the rights argument.

questions.stem: The author suggests that the three Rs framework is attractive primarily because it

options.A: guarantees that experiments that fail to meet scientific standards will be discovered and stopped before they begin.
options.B: can be accepted by people who hold conflicting views about the fundamental moral status of animals.
options.C: eliminates the need for committees to judge whether an experiment is justified in light of its likely benefits.
options.D: has been shown to reduce the number of animals used without reducing the quality of the knowledge produced.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The framework is acceptable to both utilitarians and rights theorists. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says it can become box-checking. C) The author says the underlying question gets left to a default. D) No evidence of effectiveness is cited.
questions.trap: Crediting the framework with benefits the author denies.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim about the importance of empirical questions?

options.A: Evidence that most researchers in the field describe themselves as committed to the three Rs in their published work.
options.B: Evidence that mice and monkeys differ greatly in distress under identical laboratory procedures.
options.C: Evidence that the public is more willing to support research on animals when the benefits for human health are explained.
options.D: Evidence that philosophers who defend animal rights disagree among themselves about the foundations of those rights.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Species differences in distress would show that answers about capacities depend on evidence and affect moral conclusions. Why the others are wrong: A) Self-description does not bear on empirical dependence. C) Public opinion is not part of the argument. D) Disagreement among philosophers concerns principle, not facts.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about attitudes instead of evidence about facts that bear on principles.

questions.stem: The author's statement that a badly designed study 'is wrong on every account' most clearly rests on the idea that

options.A: wasted animal suffering produces neither benefit nor respect for animals, so both utilitarian and rights-based views condemn it.
options.B: good design is sufficient to justify the use of animals, because well-designed experiments always produce valuable knowledge.
options.C: scientists bear no responsibility for demonstrating that animal work is necessary if the results are published in journals.
options.D: public examination of research is unimportant as long as investigators sympathize with the goals of science and medicine.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) A wasteful study yields no benefit and still uses animals, so it fails both approaches. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says design is necessary but does not call it sufficient. C) The author says scientists must show necessity. D) The author wants evidence the public can examine.
questions.trap: Turning a necessary condition into a sufficient one.

passages.passage_text:
Why do we punish? The question sounds childishly simple, yet each of the standard answers, taken alone, leads to conclusions that most of us would reject. The oldest answer is retribution: wrongdoers deserve to suffer in proportion to the harm they have done, and justice requires that they do. The attractions of this view are obvious. It explains why we think the punishment should fit the crime, and why we would not punish an innocent person even if doing so would calm a frightened public. But as a complete theory it has troubles. If the point of punishment is only that the guilty suffer, it is hard to say why the state, rather than the victim or an outraged crowd, should be the one to inflict it, or why suffering should be thought to balance harm that has already occurred.

A second answer looks forward. Deterrence holds that punishment is justified because the threat of it discourages crime, and incapacitation adds that confinement prevents offenders from harming others during their sentences.
