They have a clear criterion of success: less crime. Yet their weakness is the mirror image of retribution's. If the aim is only to reduce crime, it seems that we might punish an innocent person publicly to frighten others, or impose savage sentences for trivial offenses, if doing so were effective. Evidence also complicates the picture: studies repeatedly find that the certainty of being caught deters more than the severity of the penalty, which suggests that some of the harshest sentences purchase little.

Rehabilitation, the third answer, treats the offender as a person capable of change and aims to reduce reoffending through education, treatment, or work. It is humane and has some empirical support, although results vary greatly with the program and the population. Taken as the sole purpose, however, it also generates odd results. It would justify detaining someone only until a program succeeded, regardless of the gravity of the offense, and it would excuse someone who was already reformed at the time of sentencing. It tends to treat wrongdoing as a symptom to be cured, which neglects the fact that the offender, unlike a patient, has acted wrongly and may be held responsible for it.

Many contemporary writers conclude that no single purpose will do and recommend a hybrid view. One version assigns different purposes to different stages: a legislature may choose to punish certain acts in order to deter them, while the question of whom to punish is governed by desert, so that only the guilty are sentenced and none more severely than they deserve. This is a sensible compromise, but it can seem a patchwork that adds up considerations without explaining how they fit together.

A different approach, the expressive theory, may offer more unity. On this view, punishment is a form of communication: it conveys society's condemnation of the act, affirms the standing of the victim whose rights were violated, and addresses the offender as someone capable of understanding the message. Retribution survives in the claim that wrongdoing calls for a response proportionate to its seriousness; deterrence and rehabilitation survive as hoped-for effects of a message that is heard. The theory has its own difficulty, since it is not obvious why condemnation must take the form of imposing suffering rather than a formal declaration. Still, it directs attention to something the other theories miss, namely that punishment is a social act with a meaning, and that how a sentence is carried out says as much about the community as about the offender.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of the standard theories of punishment is intended primarily to show that

options.A: retribution is the only theory that can explain why the innocent should not be punished under any circumstances.
options.B: empirical evidence has settled which of the theories best explains the effects that punishment has on crime.
options.C: hybrid theories are inferior to single-purpose theories because they cannot explain how considerations fit together.
options.D: each theory, taken as the sole justification, has implications that most people would find unacceptable.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The opening says each answer taken alone leads to conclusions most would reject. Why the others are wrong: A) The author treats retribution as incomplete, and other views, including hybrids, also protect the innocent. B) The author says evidence complicates the picture and does not settle the question. C) The author calls hybrid views a sensible compromise even though they look like a patchwork.
questions.trap: Taking the weakness of one theory as the point of the whole passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a problem for deterrence-based justifications is that they

options.A: might permit punishing the innocent or imposing extreme sentences if doing so would effectively reduce crime.
options.B: cannot be tested against evidence because the effects of threats on potential offenders are impossible to measure.
options.C: depend on the claim that offenders deserve to suffer in proportion to the harm that they have caused.
options.D: assume that offenders are capable of change, which most studies of repeat offending have found to be false.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says if the aim is only crime reduction, such results seem allowed. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says deterrence has a clear criterion of success and cites studies. C) That is retribution's premise. D) That is rehabilitation's premise, and the author says results vary and some support exists.
questions.trap: Attributing the premise of one theory to another.

questions.stem: The reference to studies on certainty and severity of penalties serves to

options.A: demonstrate that deterrence is the most effective purpose of punishment according to the best available evidence.
options.B: prove that rehabilitation programs are more effective than severe sentences in lowering the rate of repeat offenses.
options.C: show that the probability of capture has no meaningful influence on the decisions of potential offenders.
options.D: suggest that some harsh sentences may produce little additional deterrence, complicating a simple deterrence rationale.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Certainty deters more than severity, so harsh sentences may buy little. Why the others are wrong: A) The evidence complicates deterrence rather than vindicating it. B) The studies do not address rehabilitation. C) The studies say certainty does matter more.
questions.trap: Reversing the finding about certainty and severity.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that the hybrid view described in the fourth paragraph

options.A: offers a workable division of purposes but does not by itself explain how the considerations are unified.
options.B: resolves the main objections to retribution by allowing the state to impose any sentence that deters crime.
options.C: is preferable to the expressive theory because it avoids treating punishment as a form of communication.
options.D: is unsound because desert cannot be used to determine whom the law should punish.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author calls it sensible but patchwork. Why the others are wrong: B) Under the hybrid view desert limits severity. C) The author finds the expressive theory possibly more unified. D) The hybrid view uses desert for whom to punish, and the author calls it sensible.
questions.trap: Missing that desert acts as a limit in the hybrid view.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly challenge the expressive theory as the passage presents it?

options.A: Evidence that sentences that are carried out in public are viewed by communities as expressing greater concern for victims.
options.B: Evidence that offenders who understand the message conveyed by their sentences are less likely to commit further offenses.
options.C: Evidence that offenders and communities read a formal public condemnation as conveying the same message as prison.
options.D: Evidence that societies differ in the severity of the penalties that they regard as appropriate for particular crimes.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) If a declaration conveys the same message, suffering seems unnecessary, which is the difficulty the author names. Why the others are wrong: A) That would support the expressive theory. B) That supports the hoped-for effects of a heard message. D) Variation in severity norms is consistent with punishment having social meaning.
questions.trap: Picking evidence that supports the theory.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage suggests that the author values the expressive theory because it

options.A: highlights that the way a sentence is carried out reflects the character of the community that imposes it.
options.B: proves that punishment is justified only when the offender fully understands the nature of the wrong committed.
options.C: shows that the offender's reform is a more important consequence of punishment than the condemnation of the act.
options.D: demonstrates that formal declarations of condemnation can replace imprisonment for most categories of offenses.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says punishment is a social act and how it is carried out says as much about the community as about the offender. Why the others are wrong: B) The author makes no such necessary condition. C) Reform is called a hoped-for effect, not the main point. D) The author notes the difficulty of why condemnation need take suffering, but does not claim declarations can replace imprisonment.
questions.trap: Overstating the author's tentative endorsement.
